newsitem.title: USA: Division over EMU, NATO is backdrop for G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Division over EMU, NATO is backdrop for G7 meeting.

text.p: G7 leaders meet this week against a backdrop of internal division, with Paris and Bonn at loggerheads over European monetary union and Washington in conflict with several of its allies over NATO expansion.

The annual summit of the Group of Seven (G7) -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- is traditionally a time to take stock of the world economy and chart collective action on political matters.

At this year's gathering, which is being held June 20-22 in Denver and will include Russian President Boris Yeltsin for nearly all its sessions, much of the action may take place outside the formal meetings.

France and Germany are divided over economic and monetary union (EMU) in Europe, with France's newly elected socialist government reluctant to commit itself to further austerity to meet the economic criteria for a single currency.

"A subtext or subtheme of the summit will be EMU," a senior U.S. official, who declined to be identified, said. "There's going to be, either explicitly or right below the surface, a lot more tension among the Europeans."

The Europeans may be able to bridge their differences over EMU at a European Union summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday, but if they do not, the matter seems likely to come up on the sidelines of the Denver meeting.
Another matter expected to surface at bilateral meetings outside the summit will be plans to invite new members to join NATO.

Defying its allies, the United States said on Thursday it wanted to invite only three nations -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin negotiations to enter the Western security alliance.
France and Germany insisted on Friday they would support Romania and Slovenia for membership despite the U.S. stance.

A senior U.S. official said President Bill Clinton would raise the issue in Denver at bilateral meetings with President Jacques Chirac of France, which has championed Romania, and Prime Minister Romano Prodi of Italy, which backs Slovenia.

U.S. officials said they expected the matter to be resolved before a July 8-9 summit in Madrid that will invite countries to begin membership talks. Clinton has set 1999, NATO's 50th anniversary, as the target date for the acceptance of new members.
The United States, host of the Denver meeting, has baptised the gathering the "Summit of the Eight" to highlight the expanded role of Russia.

Russia's Yeltsin -- who has attended every G7 summit since 1992 except last year's in Lyon, France, held when he was ill -- will take part in all the Denver meetings except a Saturday afternoon session on economic and financial matters.

In another reflection of the Russian presence, the summit is to issue only one communique instead of the usual two. This communique, in the name of the eight, will focus on political matters. A separate economic statement will reflect G7 concerns alone.

There may be disagreements among the seven on economics, with the United States, Britain and Canada enjoying strong growth while France, Germany and Italy suffer from sluggish domestic economies and double-digit unemployment.
One senior U.S. official said the situation represented a change from Clinton's first G7 summit, at Tokyo in 1993, when he was taken to task for the United States' ballooning budget deficit.
"We're actually able to say with credibility that we did set our house in order," the official said, citing the sharp decline in the U.S. budget deficit and robust U.S. growth.

"My guess is that his message to these leaders in private would be ... to make their constituencies aware that they have to, at least temporarily, adopt the painful process of adjustment if they want to produce long-term growth and long-term jobs," Bob Hormats, international vice chairman of Goldman Sachs, said.
"He (Clinton) is not going to say that in public, but it seems to me that that will be the private message," he said.
